prompt: In the Tier 3 vs. platform-engineering comparison, what is the key difference between how a developer got a namespace before the platform existed versus after?
choices: Before: filed a ticket and waited on SRE; after: a self-service request (e.g. a PR adding a directory) triggers automatic provisioning with no SRE in the loop
Before: used Helm; after: used raw kubectl apply
Before: namespaces were created automatically by Kubernetes; after: they must be requested manually
There is no real difference — the platform just adds a UI on top of the same ticket process

prompt: In GitOps, where does CI's responsibility end and the GitOps controller's responsibility begin?
choices: CI runs `helm upgrade` directly against the production cluster; the controller only reports status
CI's job stops at merging rendered state into the git repository; the controller is responsible for applying that state to the live cluster and keeping it there
CI and the controller both apply manifests to the cluster independently, and whichever runs last wins
The controller only runs once at initial cluster bootstrap; after that, CI takes over all deployments

prompt: According to the reconciliation-loop mechanism described, how does ArgoCD's application-controller know the current live state of the cluster, and how is that compared to the desired state from git?
choices: It runs `kubectl get` on a fixed polling schedule and diffs raw JSON byte-for-byte against the git YAML
It maintains Kubernetes informers that watch live resources continuously, and normalizes the diff against freshly rendered git manifests (ignoring server-managed fields) to decide Synced vs OutOfSync
It has no live-state cache; every sync re-reads the entire cluster from etcd directly
It trusts the Kubernetes audit log to tell it what changed, rather than comparing state directly

prompt: An engineer runs `kubectl edit` on a Deployment managed by an ArgoCD Application with `selfHeal: true`. What happens?
choices: The edit is permanent; ArgoCD only applies changes on new git commits
ArgoCD immediately blocks the kubectl command from succeeding
The edit takes effect temporarily, but on the next reconciliation tick the controller detects the drift against git's desired state and reverts the live object back to match git
The edit is automatically committed back into the git repository to keep git in sync with the cluster

prompt: In the `team-namespaces` ApplicationSet example using a git `directories` generator over `teams/*`, how does a brand-new team directory (e.g. `teams/recommendations/`) get turned into a running Application without editing the ApplicationSet itself?
choices: It doesn't — the ApplicationSet spec must be manually edited for every new team
The generator re-scans the `teams/*` glob on each reconcile; any new matching directory is automatically rendered through the same template into its own Application
A human must run `argocd app create` manually for each new team directory
New teams require a separate Helm chart install per team

prompt: Why does the self-service namespace flow attach a ResourceQuota to every team namespace by default, rather than letting teams request compute unbounded?
choices: ResourceQuota is required by Kubernetes for any namespace to exist
It bounds the blast radius of a team's mistake (e.g. a typo'd replica count) to a known ceiling, so self-service can be safely granted without a human reviewer in the common path
It is purely a billing/accounting label with no effect on scheduling
It replaces the need for a NetworkPolicy entirely

prompt: The module explicitly says enforcing quota/security rules as admission-time policy (e.g. OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno) so a bad manifest is rejected before merge is covered where?
choices: In this same module, in the self-service infrastructure section
It isn't covered anywhere in this curriculum
In this track's own later Tier 4 supply-chain and policy-as-code security module
In the Cybersecurity & Ethical Hacking track's Application Security Specialist path

prompt: What does the `project: payments` field on the ArgoCD Application manifest provide?
choices: It sets the Kubernetes namespace the resources are deployed into
It names the git branch the Application tracks
It scopes the Application to an AppProject, restricting which source repos and destination clusters/namespaces that team is allowed to target — a multi-tenancy guardrail
It configures the Helm chart's values file
